prompt: A rectangular piece of paper $ABCD$ has sides of lengths $AB=1$, $BC=2$. The rectangle is folded in half such that $AD$ coincides with $BC$ and $EF$ is the folding line. Then fold the paper along a line $BM$ such that the corner $A$ falls on line $EF$. How large, in degrees, is $\angle ABM$?
Tetrahedron $ABCD$ has sides of lengths, in increasing order, 7, 13, 18, 27, 36, 41. If $AB=41$, then what is the length of $CD$?

A polygon is called concave if it has at least one angle strictly greater than $180^\circ$. What is the maximum number of symmetries that an $11$-sided concave polygon can have? (A symmetry of a polygon is a way to rotate or reflect the plane that leaves the polygon unchanged.)

In the following diagram (not to scale), $A,B,C,D$ are four consecutive vertices of an $18$-sided regular polygon with center $O$. Let $P$ be the midpoint of $AC$ and $Q$ be the midpoint of $DO$. Find $\angle OPQ$ in degrees.

Lines $l$ and $m$ are perpendicular. Line $l$ partitions a convex polygon into two parts of equal area, and partitions the projection of the polygon onto $m$ into two line segments of length $a$ and $b$ respectively. Determine the maximum value of $\left\lfloor\frac{1000a}{b}\right\rfloor$. (The floor notation $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the largest integer not exceeding $x$.)

Consider the solid with $4$ triangles and $4$ regular hexagons as faces, where each triangle borders $3$ hexagons, and all the sides are of length $1$. Compute the *square* of the volume of the solid. Express your result as a reduced fraction and concatenate the numerator with the denominator (e.g., if you think that the square is $\frac{1734}{274}$, then you would submit 1734274).

You are given a convex pentagon $ABCDE$ with $AB=BC$, $CD=DE$, $\angle ABC=150^\circ$, $\angle BCD=165^\circ$, $\angle CDE=30^\circ$, $BD=6$. Find the area of this pentagon. Round your answer to the nearest integer if necessary.

solutions.title: Cut into three triangles
solutions.body:
Let $AB=BC=a$, $CD=DE=b$, $AC=p$, $CE=q$ and $\angle BCD=x$ (here $x=165^\circ$; the value of $x$ will turn out not to matter).

By the law of cosines $p^2=2a^2(1-\cos150^\circ)=2a^2(1+\cos30^\circ)$ and $q^2=2b^2(1-\cos30^\circ)$, so $p^2q^2=4a^2b^2(1-\cos^230^\circ)=a^2b^2$ and $pq=ab$.

Triangles $ABC$, $CDE$ are isosceles with base angles $15^\circ$ and $75^\circ$, so $\angle ACE=x-15^\circ-75^\circ=x-90^\circ$. The area is $$[ABC]+[CDE]+[ACE]=\tfrac12a^2\sin150^\circ+\tfrac12b^2\sin30^\circ+\tfrac12pq\sin(x-90^\circ)=\tfrac14\left(a^2+b^2-2ab\cos x\right).$$ By the law of cosines in triangle $BCD$ this is $\frac14BD^2=\frac{36}{4}=9$.

**Answer: 9**

prompt: Consider $\triangle ABC$ and a point $M$ in its interior so that $\angle MAB=10^\circ$, $\angle MBA=20^\circ$, $\angle MCA=30^\circ$ and $\angle MAC=40^\circ$. What is $\angle MBC$?

solutions.title: Trigonometric Ceva
solutions.body:
Let $\beta=\angle MBC$ and $\gamma=\angle MCB$. The angles of the triangle add to $180^\circ$: $(10^\circ+40^\circ)+(20^\circ+\beta)+(30^\circ+\gamma)=180^\circ$, so $\beta+\gamma=80^\circ$.

Trigonometric Ceva for $M$: $$\frac{\sin10^\circ}{\sin40^\circ}\cdot\frac{\sin30^\circ}{\sin\gamma}\cdot\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin20^\circ}=1.$$ Try $\beta=60^\circ$, $\gamma=20^\circ$: the left side is $\frac{\sin10^\circ\cdot\frac12\cdot\sin60^\circ}{\sin40^\circ\sin^220^\circ}$, which equals $1$: it is equivalent to $\sin10^\circ\sin60^\circ=2\sin40^\circ\sin^220^\circ$, and using $\sin20^\circ\sin40^\circ\sin80^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}8$ with $\sin80^\circ=\cos10^\circ$ the right side becomes $\frac{\sqrt3\sin20^\circ}{4\cos10^\circ}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin10^\circ$. Since $\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin(80^\circ-\beta)}$ is increasing in $\beta$ on $(0^\circ,80^\circ)$, the solution is unique, so $\beta=60^\circ$.

**Answer: 60**

solutions.title: Show $AM\perp BC$
solutions.body:
Put $M=(0,0)$ and $A=(0,1)$. Then line $BA$ makes $80^\circ$ with the horizontal, $BM$ makes $60^\circ$, $CA$ makes $50^\circ$ with the horizontal on the other side and $CM$ makes $20^\circ$ (these come from the given angles). The heights of $B$ and $C$ above $M$ are $\frac{\tan20^\circ}{\tan20^\circ-\tan50^\circ}$ and $\frac{\tan60^\circ}{\tan60^\circ-\tan80^\circ}$. They are equal iff $\tan20^\circ\tan80^\circ=\tan60^\circ\tan50^\circ$, i.e. $\tan20^\circ\tan40^\circ\tan80^\circ=\tan60^\circ$, which is the identity $\tan x\tan(60^\circ-x)\tan(60^\circ+x)=\tan3x$ at $x=20^\circ$. So $BC\perp AM$, and $\angle MBC=90^\circ-\angle MAB-\angle MBA=90^\circ-10^\circ-20^\circ=60^\circ$.

**Answer: 60**
